oral: Oral pigmentation case and follow-up
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12942211/
peer-reviewed

42-year-old man with new/darker brown gingival and buccal mucosal pigment; earlier pigment, tobacco and sunbeds remain relevant; one-/three-month follow-up; no lip, tongue or palate pigmentation in the presented case.

During Melanotan II use: bilateral brown macular attached-gingiva pigmentation and bilateral irregular buccal-mucosal macules. At 28 days: cheek regression. Three months: gingival pigment diminished but unresolved; some buccal macules remained.
Melanotan II exposure, body site, observed serial findings, and limits; not a universally expected symptom, frequency or treatment guide.
Oral pigmented lesions differential
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40369390/
peer-reviewed
Physiological, post-inflammatory, exogenous, benign-neoplastic, and malignant causes; careful clinical assessment and indicated biopsy.

The spectrum can include physiologic pigmentation, an amalgam tattoo, smoker's melanosis, post-inflammatory pigmentation, benign neoplasms and oral mucosal melanoma. While most are benign, careful clinical evaluation and when indicated biopsy matter.
Differential, not reader diagnosis or proof of a particular lesion's cause.
Separate oral melanoma case
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40210573/
peer-reviewed
22-year-old woman previously using nasal MT-II, mass upper jaw; histology confirmed oral mucosal melanoma; surgery/ongoing immunotherapy.

The patient had used the nasal spray for tanning purposes. Histological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of a mucosal malignant melanoma. The patient subsequently underwent surgical resection followed by ongoing immunotherapy.
Published case is not cancer causation or a relative-risk calculation; no dose or frequency in my copy.
NHS oral symptom escalation
https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/mouth-cancer/symptoms/
regulatory
Clinical review for >3-week ulcer, mouth/lip lump, red/white patch, persistent pain; dentist or GP; symptoms can have other common causes.
Symptoms are very common and can be caused by other conditions. Having the symptoms does not definitely mean you have mouth cancer, but it's important to get checked by a GP or dentist.
No inference from generic mouth symptoms to MT-II-specific risk. Published date on NHS is review date.
Oral melanocyte differential and biopsy
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3775277/
peer-reviewed
Oral pigmentation has varying distributions and causes requiring thorough history; biopsy when the cause cannot be identified. Used as corroboration only, no claim solely dependent on it.

A thorough investigation of dental, medical, family and social histories is necessary. If the underlying cause of the pigmentation cannot be readily identified, a tissue biopsy is essential for definitive diagnosis.
Do not adopt its older race-based generalizations or fixed biopsy approach; modern review bounds clinical context.
